title: Screens and Your Wellbeing
hook: It's not just how many hours you're on a screen — it's how and when. The same phone can leave you rested or wrecked depending on use.
key_points: Screen light and stimulation late at night can delay and worsen sleep.
Constant notifications fragment attention and make focus harder.
Passive scrolling and social comparison can drag down mood.
What you do on a screen matters as much as the total time.
content_html: Most advice about screens fixates on a single number: hours per day. Psychologists who study technology use suggest a more useful lens — the content, context, and timing of use often matter more than the raw total.
extra_html: Drawing on the American Psychological Association's guidance on technology use, the issue isn't screens as villains but specific patterns. Bright, engaging screens late at night can push back when you fall asleep and lower sleep quality. A steady drip of notifications keeps pulling your attention away, making sustained focus harder to recover. And passive, endless scrolling — especially feeds built around social comparison — is more closely tied to low mood than active, purposeful use like messaging a friend or learning something. The takeaway is empowering: rather than aiming for an arbitrary hour limit, notice which uses leave you feeling better and which leave you depleted, and shape your habits around that. If screen use is seriously affecting your mood or sleep, it's worth discussing with a clinician.

related.title: Building Healthier Screen Habits
related.hook: You don't need to quit your phone — just out-design it. A few small tweaks beat willpower for taking back your attention.

related.title: Why Sleep Matters
related.hook: Sleep isn't downtime — it's when your brain consolidates memory and your body repairs itself. Skimp on it for long and the bill comes due in your health.

related.title: What Mental Health Really Means
related.hook: Mental health isn't just the absence of illness — it's being able to cope with life's stresses, work, learn, and contribute. Everyone has it, and it can be cared for.

flashcards.prompt: Why is 'how' you use screens often more important than 'how much'?
flashcards.back_html: The same total time can help or harm depending on when and how you use it — late-night light and stimulation hurt sleep, constant notifications fragment attention, and passive scrolling and comparison can lower mood.

flashcards.prompt: Which screen pattern is most associated with disrupted sleep?

choices.text: Stimulating, bright screen use right before bed
Reading an article over morning coffee
A short video call in the afternoon

flashcards.explanation_html: Bright light and mental stimulation late at night can delay sleep onset and reduce sleep quality, which is why timing matters so much.
